setupSteps: Empty stomach. Practise about 3 to 4 hours after a heavy meal (one source says about 4 hours); a light stomach is fine.
Place. Quiet corner, fresh air but no fan blowing on you. Phone on Do Not Disturb.
Clear the nose. Blow your nose gently first. If one side stays blocked, do not force it (see Safety).

Seat. (a) Cross-legged on a folded blanket so the hips sit higher than the knees; (b) on a firm chair, feet flat, knees about hip height, back away from the backrest; or (c) on the heels (Vajrasana) if the knees are comfortable.
Left hand. On the left knee, palm up or down, thumb and index finger lightly touching if you like. Shoulder relaxed.
Right hand (Vishnu mudra). Fold the index and middle fingers gently into the palm. The thumb will close the right nostril; the ring finger (and little finger) will close the left.
Spine and head. Lift the crown of the head, keep the back of the neck long, chin level. Eyes closed or soft gaze. Relax the face, jaw and belly.
Pace. Beginner count: 4 seconds in, 4 seconds out (1:1). Use the app timer or count in your head. No holds.
Camera. Phone at chest height seated, about 1.5 to 2 m to the side, so the head, shoulders, hips and knees are in frame (see sections 11 and 12).

steps.title: Settle
steps.action: sit tall, hands in position, breathe normally through the nose.
steps.feel: seat bones pressing down, chest lifting slightly.

steps.title: Raise the right hand to the nose
steps.action: bend the right elbow and bring the thumb and ring finger to the soft sides of the nose, below the bony bridge, elbow lower than the wrist.

steps.title: Close the right nostril and empty gently
steps.action: close the right nostril with the thumb and breathe out softly through the left.
steps.feel: the right side sealed, no squeezing.

steps.title: Inhale through the left
steps.action: breathe in slowly and smoothly through the left nostril.
steps.feel: cool air along the left nostril, ribs widening, belly gently rising.

steps.title: Switch
steps.action: close the left nostril with the ring finger, then lift the thumb off the right nostril.
steps.feel: a smooth switch, no pause and no breath hold at the top.
steps.breathing: tiny natural turn; no hold for beginners.

steps.title: Exhale through the right
steps.action: breathe out slowly through the right nostril.
steps.feel: warm air, ribs softening, belly drawing in gently.
steps.tempo: 4 seconds (beginner); 8 seconds for the 1:2 ratio later.

steps.title: Inhale through the right
steps.action: breathe in slowly through the same right nostril you just breathed out of.

steps.title: Switch again
steps.action: close the right nostril with the thumb and release the left nostril.

steps.title: Exhale through the left
steps.action: breathe out slowly through the left nostril. This completes round 1.

steps.title: Repeat
steps.action: repeat steps 4 to 9 for the planned rounds (beginner 5 rounds).
steps.feel: the breath getting quieter and more even.

steps.title: Finish
steps.action: lower the right hand to the right knee, release both nostrils, eyes closed.
steps.visualCheck: relaxed jaw, hands resting on the knees.

commonMistakes.title: Forcing or sniffing the breath
commonMistakes.text: Forcing or sniffing the breath. It makes noise, tires the nose and can cause dizziness. Fix: make the breath so quiet you could not hear it an arm's length away; shorten the count.

commonMistakes.title: Holding the breath too early
commonMistakes.text: Holding the breath too early. Breath retention can raise blood pressure and heart rate during the hold (review table PMC10989416; a pilot study found systolic pressure rose during 30-second holds). Fix: no holds for beginners; any retention only with a qualified teacher.

commonMistakes.title: Pressing hard on the nose or the bony bridge
commonMistakes.text: Pressing hard on the nose or the bony bridge. It hurts and can bend the cartilage. Fix: use the soft sides, the lightest touch.

commonMistakes.title: Slouching or leaning back
commonMistakes.text: Slouching or leaning back. It squashes the diaphragm so the breath feels short. Fix: sit on a cushion or chair; stack ears over shoulders over hips.

commonMistakes.title: Raising the shoulder and elbow high
commonMistakes.text: Raising the shoulder and elbow high. It tires the arm and neck. Fix: keep the right elbow low, or support it with the left hand.

commonMistakes.title: Unequal counts or speeding up
commonMistakes.text: Unequal counts or speeding up. An in-breath longer than the out-breath feels breathless. Fix: use the timer cue; keep the exhale at least as long as the inhale.

commonMistakes.title: Practising with a full stomach, a blocked nose or when ill
commonMistakes.text: Practising with a full stomach, a blocked nose or when ill. It feels hard and uncomfortable. Fix: wait, clear the nose gently, or use plain slow breathing.

commonMistakes.title: Doing too much on day one
commonMistakes.text: Doing too much on day one. Tiredness or lightheadedness. Fix: start with 5 rounds (about 2 minutes) and add 1 to 2 rounds a week.

safetyNotes: Soft and silent, never strained. The breath should feel easy; air hunger, dizziness or noise means you are pushing too hard.

Breath retention (kumbhaka): a review table on yoga for hypertension (PMC10989416) says retention raises systolic and diastolic pressure and mean arterial pressure because heart rate and resistance both rise, and advises against long retention in hypertension. A guide says people who are pregnant, have high blood pressure or heart disease, or a condition affecting breathing or consciousness should speak to a health professional before breath retention. Beginners should not hold their breath at all.
Blocked nose, cold, sinus infection or nosebleeds: skip, or use plain slow breathing.

Pregnancy: the Government of India WCD "Yoga for Pregnant Ladies" guide lists alternate nostril breathing but advises skipping breath retention and fast breathing. Gentle only, supported sitting, check with the doctor or midwife. A pregnancy trial of this practice: Not found.
High blood pressure and heart disease: no breath holding; ask a doctor first, especially with heart disease; keep taking medicine.

Asthma and COPD: ask a doctor; gentle pace, no forced or fast breathing, keep the reliever inhaler nearby; skip during an attack or cold. Small studies of pranayama in asthma were seen only in search summaries and a registered trial (NCT07529847) has no results; Anulom Vilom-specific asthma evidence: Not found.

Other cautions: vertigo, fainting, panic attacks (stop if lightheaded); recent chest or abdominal surgery (ask the surgeon); back or knee problems (sit on a chair). Wellness blogs list dizziness and muscle strain as possible risks when done too fast or incorrectly (snippets).

Stop immediately if you feel: dizziness, tingling in the hands or lips, chest pain or tightness, wheeze or unusual shortness of breath, a faint feeling, sudden headache, or pain in the nose or ears. Return to natural breathing; if it continues, seek medical help.
Spotter: not needed. Gym etiquette: not relevant; if practising in a gym studio, keep the space quiet.

Ratio: 1:1 then 1:2 (beginner guides) versus 1:3:2 (one study) versus 1:4:2 (traditional text via a pharmacy blog). We chose 1:1 then 1:2 with no retention.
Anulom Vilom versus Nadi Shodhana: some sources say the first has no holds and the second adds them; the CYP uses both names. We chose no holds.
Blood pressure: a meta-analysis and a 5-day trial report drops; a healthy-volunteer trial found no significant change. We describe it as possible, small and uncertain.
MET: no pranayama code found; we chose Hatha yoga 02150 = 2.3 as the nearest confirmed code and flagged it as an upper bound.

Not found: the AYUSH/MDNIY technique text and its definition of a round; a 2024 Compendium pranayama, meditation or sitting-quietly code; official joint angles for seated posture; Anulom Vilom-specific asthma trial results; pregnancy trial evidence; strong evidence for sleep benefit; condition sources for high cholesterol, obesity, knee pain, lower back pain, shoulder problems, osteoporosis, postpartum, recent surgery, and thyroid. Our thresholds are estimates.
Most pages were seen only as search snippets or summaries; direct page fetches were not possible, so effect sizes are as reported in abstracts or tables.
